title: Pardons Mary Ballard McCarty
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Mary Ballard McCarty as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted a pardon to Mary Ballard McCarty, whose case was in the Southern District of Florida. The Justice Department lists her 2009 sentence as 42 months in prison, three years of supervised release and a $100,000 fine for conspiracy to commit honest-services fraud.
description_long: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted a pardon to Mary Ballard McCarty, whose federal case was in the Southern District of Florida. The Justice Department’s clemency record lists a 42-month prison sentence, three years of supervised release and a $100,000 fine imposed in 2009 for conspiracy to commit honest-services fraud. The pardon appeared among the grants issued during the final days of Trump’s first term. A presidential pardon is an act of executive clemency for a federal offense; it does not amount to a new trial or erase the historical record of the conviction. The announcement did not explain why McCarty was selected. A pardon can remove some collateral consequences of a federal conviction, but it does not turn the underlying proceedings into an acquittal or erase the court record.

title: Election Certification Interference - Training Trump Supporters to Block Results
description_short: Election Certification Interference - Training Trump Supporters to Block Results
description_medium: Newsweek reported that election officials in battleground states warned counties not to stop certification. The report said law professor David Clements organized events attended by thousands of Trump supporters in at least 40 counties across more than a dozen states, where participants were taught to pressure local officials. It did not report a county refusing to certify as a result.
description_long: Donald Trump and his allies systematically trained supporters across battleground states to pressure local election officials into refusing to certify election results, creating a coordinated infrastructure to steal elections through procedural sabotage at the county level. Law professor David Clements, a prominent election fraud conspiracy theorist, organized events with thousands of attendees across more than 40 counties in over a dozen states, including critical battlegrounds like Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania, teaching Trump supporters how to intimidate certification officials. The training sessions focused on exploiting the ministerial duty of certification by encouraging Trump supporters to claim fraud without evidence and demand that county commissioners refuse to certify results, potentially disenfranchising entire counties. State election officials responded by issuing stern warnings that certification is mandatory, with Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes stating that counties failing to certify 'risk facing indictment.' The interference campaign built on lessons from 2020, when some Trump-supporting election officials attempted to delay or refuse certification before ultimately being forced to comply with their legal duties. Federal and state courts had already ruled that certification is a ministerial function that election officials cannot refuse based on personal beliefs about fraud, but Trump's network continued training supporters to pressure officials into violating these legal requirements. The systematic training represents an unprecedented attempt to steal elections through coordinated local-level sabotage of the certification process.

title: UN mission finds reasonable grounds for U.S. war crimes in Minab and Lamerd strikes
description_short: UN mission finds reasonable grounds for U.S. war crimes in Minab and Lamerd strikes
description_medium: On September 17, 2026, UN-appointed investigators reported reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed war crimes in two February strikes on civilian facilities in Iran, at Minab and Lamerd. The assessment was not a criminal conviction. BBC reported U.S. denials concerning Lamerd and said the mission’s Minab investigation had not been released.
description_long: On September 17, 2026, a United Nations fact-finding mission reported reasonable grounds to believe that the United States committed war crimes in two February strikes on civilian facilities in Iran, at Minab and Lamerd. The finding was an investigative assessment, not a criminal conviction or a judgment by a court. BBC reporting described evidence considered by the mission and noted U.S. denials concerning the Lamerd strike. The mission’s investigation into Minab had not been released, so the public account did not present the evidence or conclusions for that strike in the same way. The distinction between the two incidents matters: the report summarized a reasonable-grounds assessment for both, while the underlying public detail differed. The announcement concerned findings about earlier military actions, not new strikes on September 17. It raised questions about responsibility for attacks on civilian facilities and about what further investigation or legal review might follow. No later court outcome or criminal judgment is established by the supplied material.
organization_tags: UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran
